backups.overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.
backups.beta: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
backups.turnaround: Because the upper mountain is loose scree/talus with real rockfall and slip potential, and the approach is long and entirely off-trail through remote wilderness, set a firm turnaround time before starting the summit push and commit to it — visibility loss (fog/cloud) on the unmarked upper slopes is the biggest threat to a safe descent, and there is no faster way down than the way up.

backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is documented for this route — it is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no glacier travel per the published route description.
backups.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, roughly 16-20 miles one-way depending on the line chosen, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it has been closed to vehicles at Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Seattle Creek Basin or Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach (Elwha side) follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
backups.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
backups.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness permit reservation: $6 reservation fee plus $8 per person per night for climbers/backpackers age 16+ (15 and under free), as of 2026.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Hard-sided, approved bear-resistant food canisters are required for all overnight stays throughout most of Olympic Wilderness, including the Elwha and Quinault interior zones; bear wires/hangs are not accepted. There is no separate climbing registration — rangers do not certify competency or refuse a permit for lack of gear/experience, so self-sufficiency and route knowledge are entirely on the party.
access.permit: A backcountry wilderness camping permit is required for any overnight stay and must be reserved through recreation.gov before your trip.
access.closures: Olympic Hot Springs Road beyond Madison Falls has been closed to vehicles since November 2017 flood damage, with no reopening date on Olympic National Park's alerts page updated August 27, 2026, adding roughly 7 miles each way of walking or biking to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead on the Elwha approach. On the Quinault side, South Shore Road has a separate washout closure near milepost 8 (use North Shore Road as the detour); North Shore Road itself also had a seasonal construction closure near milepost 10.2 (culvert replacement, closed July 9–Sept 22, 2025). Call the park's Road and Weather Hotline (360-565-3131) or check nps.gov/olym for current status before committing to either approach.

climate.summer: The most reliable window (Jul-Sep) but still unsettled — trip reports document rain and hail squalls even in early September
climate.winter: Heavy snow and storms make the multi-day approach and summit slopes impractical for most parties
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: wet, mild winters with heavy snow accumulation in the high interior, and a relatively short, more stable summer window. The standard scramble is typically driest and most snow-free from mid-July through September.

bySeason.summer: Best window (Jul-Sep) for the scree/talus scramble; expect long daylight but still-frequent Pacific frontal systems and afternoon cloud buildup typical of the Olympics.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and frequent storms make the approach trails themselves a serious undertaking; not a realistic season for this route.

emergency.notes: Call 911. This is a deep-wilderness route with a multi-day approach; expect little to no reliable cell coverage along the trail or near the summit, and plan for a slow, multi-day self-rescue or evacuation timeline.

emergency.nearestHospital: Olympic Medical Center, Port Angeles (typical evacuation point for the Elwha-side approach) or Forks Community Hospital, a Level IV trauma center (western approaches); given the multi-day walk-out from either standard approach, serious injuries are usually evacuated by helicopter (Airlift Northwest) rather than on foot.

approach_variants.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
approach_variants.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.

Extreme remoteness with emergency contact frequently impossible
approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Seattle Meadows
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

gear: rack to 3in with cams doubled on 0.5/0.75/1/2in

backups.overview: Bear Mountain's North Buttress is a serious, remote alpine rock route deep in North Cascades National Park near the Canadian border, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Mark Fielding in July 1967 (originally rated NCCS V, F8, A4; now typically climbed free around 5.10). It offers sustained, high-quality climbing up the steep, glaciated buttress in an extremely committing setting near the head of the Chilliwack/Bear Creek drainage. Note: unlike some older references claim, this route is not part of Steve Roper and Allen Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America list.
backups.beta: The most commonly climbed route on Bear Mountain's north face, established by Beckey and Fielding in 1967. The approach gains a glacier couloir on the west side of the north buttress. The upper buttress features seven roped pitches of excellent quality granitic rock with consistent protection. Route is usually climbed as a 2-3 day alpine adventure including a multi-day approach and descents.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if weather deteriorates significantly, if daylight remaining is less than 4 hours, or if any party member shows signs of severe altitude or exertion stress. This remote location has no rescue resources nearby.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell service should be expected at any point on this route. Bear Mountain is a remote, roadless area within North Cascades National Park. Satellite communicators or emergency beacons are strongly recommended.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard (non-buttress) route, downclimbing a short 3rd-class gully; no rappels are required.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail 674)
waypoints.note: End of FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) off Mt. Baker Highway; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk, and this is the start of the long multi-day approach toward Bear Creek.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and follow it to the road end at about 3,100 ft, where Hannegan Pass Trail #674 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk here.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow saddle where Hannegan Pass Trail meets the Chilliwack River Trail; leave the maintained tread here and drop north into the Chilliwack River valley toward Canada.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #674 up the valley, nearly level for the first mile and then at a steady grade, roughly 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the broad meadow saddle of the pass. Figure 2.5 to 3 hours.

waypoints.name: Bear Creek Camp (Chilliwack River Trail)
waypoints.note: Established camp at the Bear Creek confluence on the Chilliwack River Trail, the jump-off point for the Bear Mountain approach; NPS closed this camp after the 2021 Bear Creek Fire, so verify current access before counting on it.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the east side of the pass and continue about 5 miles down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the national park boundary where the Chilliwack River Trail proper begins. The tread loses elevation past U.S. Cabin camp to the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-cable car and a serious ford in high water, then runs down-valley past the Copper Creek and Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8 to 9 hours from the car. Check current status of the Bear Creek camp, which the Park Service closed after the 2021 fire.

waypoints.name: Meadows above Ruta Lake
waypoints.note: From Bear Creek, climb steep timber then huckleberry slopes east to treeline; the route gains the divide crest in open meadowland just above Ruta Lake.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at Bear Creek and ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing during snowmelt. Climb east into steep, brushy timber; higher the brush gives way to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows at about 5,800 ft above Ruta Lake.

waypoints.name: NW Ridge saddle high camp (6,480')
waypoints.note: Traverse loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822, crossing a rock rib, to this saddle on Bear's NW ridge — the standard bivy for the North Buttress, roughly 21 miles and two days from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the divide from the meadows, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to the broad saddle at 6,480 ft on Bear's northwest ridge. This is the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites, about 21 miles from the trailhead, usually reached on the second day.

waypoints.name: Glacier couloir base below North Buttress
waypoints.note: About 1.5 hours below camp; loose rock and occasional icefall/rockfall off the shrinking glacier remnant in the couloir make early starts and helmets essential here.
waypoints.directions: The route begins by losing height: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle and cross several minor gullies to the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the north buttress, about 60 to 90 minutes. An axe and crampons are worth their weight here even in summer. Loose rock and occasional icefall out of the shrinking glacier make an early start and helmets the norm.

waypoints.name: Bear Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit horn gained via seven pitches of 5.10 climbing up the buttress above the couloir; descend west on the south side of the crest, then downclimb a short 3rd-class gully back toward the saddle camp.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into the slabs leading to the corner system where the technical climbing starts, watching for a moat where the snow meets rock. Seven pitches up to 5.10a follow the crest, with the off-width crux on pitch four and easier alternatives on the crest, to the top of the buttress; a scramble from there gains the true summit.

backups.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from small (~0.4in) up to 3in max, DOUBLED on the 0.5in, 0.75in, 1in, and 2in sizes — this specific doubling comes directly from a route-focused trip report and gear list, not a generic guess. Bring a set of stoppers/nuts for thinner, more delicate placements on the 5.6-5.10a pitches. No pitons needed on modern ascents (historic 1960s FA account mentions pins, but current parties climb it clean).
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for the 2-3 day approach
food and fuel for a multi-day trip
water treatment (approach is via Chilliwack River Trail, largely unmaintained past the US/Canada border)
pro_tips: Treat this as a multi-day expedition given the approach
Strong route-finding and rappel management are essential
backups.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate on the upper buttress's crack systems across the 7 pitches (5.6-5.10a); doubled mid-size cams (0.5-2in) cover the bulk of placements, with the 5.10a section being the crux and best-protected pitch. The approach glacier couloir below the buttress crest is loose, unprotectable 4th-class snow/rock/debris terrain with rockfall exposure — no gear is placed there, move efficiently and avoid lingering below parties.
backups.best_season: Mid-summer through early fall for the most stable rock and weather.
backups.aid_grade: A4 historically at the 1967 first ascent (44 pitons, 1 bolt, through an unprotectable overhanging crack); route is now climbed free
backups.approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (~3,100 ft, end of Ruth Creek Rd/FR-32) follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 — nearly level for the first mile, then a steady grade — about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), roughly 2.5-3 hours. Drop off the back (east) side of the pass and continue about 5 more miles, bearing right at the North Cascades National Park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper; this section loses elevation into the valley, passes U.S. Cabin backcountry camp, and reaches the Chilliwack River crossing (historically a hand-cable car — verify current status with the NPS, since a high-water ford here is a real hazard). Continue down-valley past Copper Creek/Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8-9 hours from the trailhead including the pass. At Bear Creek, leave the maintained trail: ford Bear Creek (can be a genuine, sketchy crossing during snowmelt) and climb steep, brushy timber eastward. Above treeline the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake; from there traverse the divide, skirting the south slopes of Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft — the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites. All told this is roughly 21 miles and about 6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, which most parties split over two days, camping on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek because the Bear Creek camp has been closed since the 2021 fire. A much shorter line (~9 miles to camp) starts from Chilliwack Lake Road in BC, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles; the Hannegan approach is the one to plan on. From high camp, the route itself begins with a descent: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle, cross several minor gullies, and reach the toe of the small glacier/névé spilling from the couloir below the North Buttress (about 60-90 minutes); crampons and an axe are genuinely useful here even in summer. Climb the glacier/névé on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into slabs leading to the corner system that marks the start of the technical climbing, staying alert for a moat where the névé meets rock.
backups.descent_text: The standard descent off Bear Mountain's summit is a walk-off, not a rappel-mandatory line: traverse west/southwest staying on the south side of the summit crest, cross a notch/gap, and work across a snowfield that breaks the cliff bands above the Bear Creek drainage, then continue down easier 3rd-4th class terrain. A short, sometimes-loose 3rd class gully drops back down to the saddle camp at ~6,480 ft — about 1 hour and 1,400-1,500 ft of descent in good conditions. That said, this gully is exposed enough that a meaningful number of parties choose to back it up rather than down-climb it, especially with wet rock, a less-experienced partner, or an alpine-start-to-dusk timeline: a party that prefers not to downclimb it can rappel off natural anchors, though no rappel is required. There are no fixed bolted anchors on this remote, lightly-trafficked route — build natural anchors (horns, gear placements, slung blocks) and back up any old tat you find in place before weighting it. Below the gully, reverse the approach: regain the saddle, traverse back past Points 6822/6592 into the meadows above Ruta Lake, descend through brush and timber to re-ford Bear Creek, and rejoin the Chilliwack River Trail for the long hike back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Bailing from high on the buttress is serious; rappelling the route is difficult, so committing parties should be confident.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep corner just left of the crest; feels closer to 5.9+ with a heavy pack.
Fun, moderate climbing directly on the buttress crest.
Steep rock left of the crest to the ledge used by Beckey and Fielding as a bivy on the first ascent, leading into an off-width crack.
The technical crux: an off-width crack with surprisingly positive, crimpy holds; an easier 5.8 alternative exists via the buttress crest.
Blocks and cracks on the crest continuing to the base of a steep step.
Airy, exhilarating face climbing directly on the crest with perfectly positioned holds; an easier tension-traverse alternative exists.
Blocky climbing to the top of the buttress, from where it's a scramble to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed July-September once the Chilliwack River crossing has dropped and the Bear Creek ford and approach gullies are manageable. The page is built on the US approach over Hannegan Pass; a North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is needed for every night past the pass, and the Bear Creek camp has been closed since the 2021 fire, so plan the first night elsewhere on the Chilliwack River Trail.

backups.rope_note: Descent from the North Buttress (Beckey/Fielding 1967 route, aka 'North Face Buttress') is reported as a 3rd/4th class scramble/walk back to camp — no technical rappels are known on the standard descent, so a single 60m rope is standard; doubles/half ropes are unnecessary unless bailing mid-route.
backups.corrections: Existing gear text was flagged auto-generated/unverified. Verified against a route-specific trip report (Steph Abegg): the correct rack is doubles on 0.5, 0.75, 1, and 2in cams up to 3in max (not a vague 'rack to 3 inches' with no doubling detail), and the rope is a SINGLE 60m rope, not double/half ropes — descent is a 3rd/4th class walk/scramble back to camp with no technical rappels documented, so there is no reason to carry doubles. Also confirmed the approach 'glacier couloir' is loose, unprotectable 4th-class snow/rock/debris terrain (rockfall hazard, move fast) rather than crevassed glacier travel requiring a crevasse-rescue kit.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW AT CAMP. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS UPWARD FROM THE SADDLE TOWARD ROCK IS THE WRONG ONE.

IDENTIFY THE SADDLE FIRST: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

AT THE ICE, THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE BUTTRESS YOU GO UP. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS ITSELF, WHERE THE ROCK MEETS THE ICE ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE, IS THE START OF THE DIRECT AND NOT OF THIS ROUTE. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

WATCH THE JOIN BETWEEN SNOW AND ROCK. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A CROSS-CHECK ONCE COMMITTED: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH VARIANT CHANGES ONLY HOW YOU ARRIVE AT THE 6,480 FT SADDLE. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by DROPPING off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

THE SAME TWO TESTS APPLY AT THE ICE. Go up the snow on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE MARKER: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

bivy.name: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively the only high camp for the buttress, in heather meadow a little below the notch on the northwest ridge, where scattered trees give some wind shelter and flat grassy ground. Reached by climbing roughly 3,000 ft out of the Bear Creek valley to treeline on a rough climbers' path through open forest that gives way to blueberry brush. Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.
bivy.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.

backups.overview: Bear Mountain's Direct North Buttress climbs the full buttress in one continuous push -- roughly 21 pitches of sustained crack and face climbing to 5.10-, first established by Alan Kearney and Bobby Knight over two and a half days in September 1980, and later freed by Bryan Burdo and Yann Merrand in 1985. Unlike the original 1967 Beckey-Fielding line, which reaches the upper buttress via a glacier couloir, the Direct start climbs the lower buttress from its toe, in the same remote, committing setting near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park.
backups.beta: Established by Alan Kearney and Bobby Knight over 2.5 days in September 1980, the Direct North Buttress adds roughly seven difficult 5.10 pitches up the previously-unclimbed lower buttress before joining Beckey and Fielding's 1967 line on the upper buttress. Standout lower-buttress features include a 300-ft dihedral with a roof, a 130-ft hand-and-fist crack, and an off-width; the route finishes via the shared upper-buttress pitches to the crest.
backups.turnaround: Because the route is long (21 pitches) and rescue is far away, set a clear turnaround based on pace through the lower pitches to avoid finishing the upper buttress after dark or in worsening weather.
backups.rappels: None — walk-off descent, single rope sufficient
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage; a remote wilderness setting abutting the Canadian border.
backups.descent: Leave the rack and rope near the top of the route, solo easy terrain to the summit, then descend snow slopes through cliff bands back toward camp.

timing.recommendedStart: Alpine start from saddle camp; historically climbed over ~2.5 days including a bivy

backups.detailed_rack: Full rack from small nuts/finger-size cams up through a BD #4 (~4in) — the #4 is specifically noted as 'helpful on the lower crux.' Bring doubles of the mid-range cams (roughly 0.4-2in) to cover sustained, varied crack sizes across the route's 21 pitches, including the P3 5.10- roof and the awkward P16a 5.10- offwidth (harder with a loaded pack).
what_to_bring: lightweight ice axe (helpful for a steep snow section near the route base, not mandatory)
multi-day bivy/approach gear (2-3 day approach via the largely unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail past the US/Canada border)
extra water capacity (upper-pitch snowmelt is unreliable)
pro_tips: The lower seven 5.10 pitches are the technical crux — many parties still opt for the easier glacier-couloir start of the original route instead
Doubles in mid-size cams speed progress on the traversing, sparsely-protected pitches
backups.pro_needs: Protection is generally good throughout on solid Cascades rock, with doubled mid-size cams covering most placements and the BD #4 specifically useful low on the route. Watch the P6 leftward traverse past loose blocks — described as 'sketchy' and a real rockfall hazard, protect and communicate carefully there. Upper pitches can be wet from snowmelt depending on season.
backups.best_season: Mid-summer through early fall for the most stable rock and weather, matching the regional window for this peak.
backups.approach: Bear Mountain sits deep in the Chilliwack Range and is reached almost entirely on foot from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead: hike over Hannegan Pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail down-valley, then leave the maintained trail at the Bear Creek confluence and climb steep brushy timber to the meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide to a high camp on the broad saddle near 6,480 ft. From camp the Direct is reached by dropping to the glacier remnant below the wall and tying in where the toe of the buttress meets the snow; the descent from the summit returns to the same camp. The trailhead-to-camp leg is roughly 21 miles and 6,500 ft of gain, usually split over two days with a night on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek, because the camp at the Bear Creek confluence has been closed since the 2021 fire. Round trips typically run 5-6 days, about 45 miles and roughly 12,000 ft of gain.
backups.descent_text: Climbers typically leave their rack and rope near the top of the technical climbing, then solo easy terrain to Bear Mountain's summit before descending snow slopes through cliff bands back toward the high camp.
backups.bail: The lower seven pitches offer limited retreat with sparse protection; the easiest bail is before committing above the roof/dihedral section low on the route.

pitch_detail.notes: From the toe of the buttress, go right up slabs, then trend left into a broken slabby wall seamed with cracks. Climb the cracks to a recessed belay. The rock low on the buttress is poor in places; the couloir to the left is the loose, rockfall-prone alternative this start avoids.

Climb the crack in the dihedral to a roof. The crack widens toward the roof; stay in it until below the roof, then move out right, where a good hold helps. Pull through to a small ledge belay. A #4 cam is the piece that makes this pitch comfortable.
Continue up the corner system to the base of a chimney, then climb the chimney system; the two pitches can be linked. Stacked flakes lead into the chimney, so test before weighting.

Traverse left past loose blocks, which is the most unpleasant ground on the route, then back right through thin cracks with sparse protection. Ledge systems and easy but poorly protected ground follow. Protect the follower on the traverses and keep the rope clear of loose blocks.

Climb the ridge toward the snow patch; the rock here is often wet from melt. Beyond the snow, climb the face behind it by a left-hand crack to join the original 1967 North Buttress line. Crampons are recommended and a light axe helps for the snow.
A strenuous left-facing corner with a crack running from hands to fists, steep and sustained for much of a long pitch. The rock quality improves markedly from here up. Bring wide hand and fist sizes.
Two pitches up the buttress crest to the ledge at the base of the offwidth, where the 1967 party bivouacked.

16a climbs the offwidth, awkward with a pack, past some fixed gear; it is graded from 5.10a to 5.10-. 16b is the bypass: start up the offwidth, then trend right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8 and belay above the wide section.
Climb the buttress crest on steep, airy face holds with big exposure. Belay below the long crack system above.
A long series of thin cracks, close to a full rope length, to a small stance. The rock here is lichen-covered; expect it to feel harder when damp.

Easier blocky ground up the buttress to the ridgeline. Many parties leave the rope here and move up Class 4 and easy 5th, trending right to the summit ridge. Descend west on Class 3-4 ground, then snow and cliff bands back to camp.

backups.itinerary: Days 1-2: over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River Trail to camp near Brush Creek (the Bear Creek camp is closed), then ford Bear Creek and climb past Ruta Lake to the saddle camp (~6,480 ft). Days 3-4: climb the 21-pitch buttress (historically done in about 2.5 days with a bivy), then descend to camp. Days 5-6: hike back out over Hannegan Pass, about 21 miles.

July.reason: Snow clears from the divide traverse and the lower buttress dries later in the month; the glacier remnant at the toe is easiest to cross now.

June.reason: The high traverse and Ruta Lake meadows are still deep in snow and the north-facing buttress stays wet and iced.

August.reason: The most reliable month for dry rock on the shaded north face and settled weather for a multi-day remote trip; wildfire smoke is possible.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRECT STARTS AT THE VERY BOTTOM OF THE ROCK, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE ROUTE IT SHARES A CAMP WITH. From the saddle you first go DOWN: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS LIES ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THAT ICE, WHERE THE ROCK RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW. THAT JUNCTION IS THE START. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: THE REGULAR NORTH BUTTRESS WALKS PAST THIS TOE AND CONTINUES UP THE GLACIER ON THE BUTTRESS'S CLIMBER'S-LEFT SIDE, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING ON SNOW WITH THE BUTTRESS RISING TO YOUR RIGHT, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE DIRECT AND ARE HEADING FOR THE REGULAR START. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A SECOND CHECK IS HOW SOON IT GETS HARD. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

WATCH THE MOAT AT THE JUNCTION. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, which this page cannot say is lawful, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL DIFFERS, THE START DOES NOT. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

TIE IN AT THE TOE OF THE ROCK ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE ICE, WHERE THE BUTTRESS RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW AND THERE IS NO MORE SNOW ABOVE YOU. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

climbing_route.label: Lower buttress start
climbing_route.notes: The direct start takes the buttress head-on rather than escaping into the glacier couloir on the left, and that is the reason to be here: the couloir alternative is loose and largely unprotectable, with rockfall a repeated problem, while the buttress rock is clean and takes gear. Two slabby pitches on cracks around 5.8 lead to the crux roof at 5.10-. Grade V overall, about 2,200 ft and 21 pitches — this is a full day of climbing on top of a multi-day approach, so start early and know your bail options, which are poor.

climbing_route.label: Chimneys and rightward traverses
climbing_route.notes: Chimney systems above the roof lead into a series of traverses. The traversing pitches hold loose blocks and are the section most often called out as unpleasant: a block pulled here goes onto the belayer and onto anyone below, and traversing ground is also where a fall is worst for the follower. Extend runners, protect the second, and take care over what you weight.

climbing_route.label: Mid-buttress face climbing
climbing_route.notes: Face climbing and a left-hand crack system carry the route up the middle of the wall. This is where the rock can be wet from snowmelt draining the upper mountain — the same holds that are positive dry become slick, and the slabbier sequences are the ones that suffer. A cool, dry spell before the trip matters more here than on most Cascade rock.

climbing_route.label: Offwidth on the crest
climbing_route.notes: The buttress crest gives the second crux, an offwidth that is awkward with a pack on and has some fixed gear in it. A variation starts up the offwidth and then traverses right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8, belaying back at the top of the wide section — worth knowing about if the leader is climbing with a haul-free pack. A large cam (to about a 4) is the piece that makes the direct version comfortable.

climbing_route.label: Upper buttress to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Above the offwidth the crest continues at 5.9, then a long pitch of thin cracks around 5.10- to a small stance, and the remaining pitches ease off along the buttress to the ridgeline. From there most parties unrope and move together up fourth and easy fifth class ground, trending right, to gain the ridge that runs left to the summit. Rack: a full set of cams to a 4 with doubles in the mid sizes and plenty of slings; a single rope is enough because the descent is a walk-off. Descent goes west on third and fourth class terrain, roughly an hour, then down a short third-class gully to the north and through snow slopes and cliff bands back to camp — do this in daylight if at all possible, as the cliff bands are the part that goes wrong in the dark.

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
bivy.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2022 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. The 2021 and 2022 fires closed camps and trails on this side of the pass for long stretches, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was closed for a time after the 2021 and 2022 fires, so confirm its status before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

backups.name: North Peak
gear: Rope and a small rack (slings, small cams/nuts) for the chimney and rappels
Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach
Extra webbing for building 2 rappel anchors
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the North/Middle col
Loose rock in the chimney/ramp system
No established trail or cairned route — routefinding is on you
Committing rappel descent with only fixed-anchor slings of unknown age at some stations
backups.overview: Contrary to this route's name, the historic Three Fingers fire lookout actually sits on the South Peak, not here — the North Peak is a separate, harder objective and is widely considered (though not unanimously, per conflicting elevation surveys) the true high point of the mountain. There is no maintained trail, no ladders, and no register cabin; it's a roped alpine scramble/climb reached via glacier travel from Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap, with genuine exposure and no easy bail once committed to the upper chimney.
backups.beta: Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.
backups.turnaround: Turn around before committing to the crux chimney move if weather, rockfall, or party pace put a safe return to the glacier and long road-walk-out in doubt.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Boulder River Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the approach basin or on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake / Three Fingers Trailhead (Trail #641)
waypoints.note: Trailhead on Tupso Pass Spur Rd (FR 4160) off FR 41; no permit required, but the access road has a permanent washout past the Canyon Creek bridge that adds miles of foot/bike travel to reach here.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake
waypoints.note: Soggy subalpine lake with an Everett Mountaineers-built shelter at its meadow edge; camping is banned within 200 ft of the lake and campfires are prohibited from here upward.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #641 uphill from the parking area on a steady forest grade, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams on the way. Routefinding is straightforward and the lake arrives as an abrupt soggy opening rather than a viewpoint. Fill bottles here, since this is the last easy water before the alpine part of the route.

waypoints.name: Goat Flats
waypoints.note: Broad open meadow atop the ridge and the standard basecamp for the climb, about 2.5 mi below the lookout; reliable snowmelt tarns nearby but can dry out late season.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly two more miles past the lake, gaining out of the timber and onto the crest of the ridge before the trail opens into subalpine meadow with views west toward Puget Sound. Campfires are prohibited from the lake upward, so plan a stove-only camp when you stop.

waypoints.name: Tin Can Gap
waypoints.note: Trail crisscrosses the ridge to gain this notch; marks the end of maintained tread and the start of technical scrambling toward the peaks.
waypoints.directions: From the meadows the trail contours and climbs about two more miles, crisscrossing the ridge crest as it works north. Snow lies across this stretch well into summer and can bury the tread entirely, so carry an axe and expect to navigate by terrain rather than by trail. The gap gives the first full view of the three summits and the glacier below; do not continue past it without snow gear and routefinding experience, as this is where parties have needed rescue.

waypoints.name: South Peak lookout ladders
waypoints.note: Three wooden ladders rebarred and wired into the rock climb past the South Peak lookout pinnacle; exposed and can be icy early season, and this is the section the descent text means by 'downclimb the ladders.'
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail and drop roughly 400 feet off the far side of the gap on snow or talus onto the upper glacier, then traverse and climb back up to the saddle beneath the South Peak lookout pinnacle. Early in the year this is a straightforward snow descent and re-ascent; later it goes to bare ice with a moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock, and getting on and off the ice is the awkward part. The ladders start from the rock immediately above that saddle.

waypoints.name: Queest-Alb Glacier headwall crossing
waypoints.note: Route drops onto the north side of the ridge near the top of the Queest-Alb Glacier; a slip on the icy headwall runs out toward crevasses lower on the glacier.
waypoints.directions: Continuing to the true summit means leaving the lookout and dropping back off the ridge onto the north side of the glacier, generally by a gully and rocky moraine rather than straight down. Rope up and watch the runout: the slope above the crevassed lower glacier holds ice by late season and a slip does not stop on its own. Most parties turn around at the lookout, so expect no boot track from here on.

waypoints.name: Col between Middle and North Finger
waypoints.note: Traverse across the glacier gains this col between the Middle and North Fingers, the jump-off point for the West Couloir onto North Peak's South Face.
waypoints.directions: Traverse north across the glacier below the Middle Finger, then climb roughly a thousand feet of snow to the notch; the eastern of the gullies leading up takes steps well when it is firm. Crampons and an axe are wanted, and small crevasses open along the traverse as the season goes on. The col is the last flat ground, so sort gear there before starting up the rock.

waypoints.name: North Peak, Three Fingers
waypoints.note: True summit (Class 4, 5.4 variation), topped out via the West Couloir and South Face above the col; descend by reversing the snow slopes, trail, and ladders.
waypoints.directions: From the col climb the West Couloir onto the South Face, starting on loose third and fourth class rock where anyone above will send debris down. Follow the ramp on the ridge to a chimney holding the hardest moves, exposed fourth to low fifth class and worth a rope and a few slings; a direct line on the upper west face is harder still at about 5.4. Above the chimney the angle eases to class 2-3, but a false summit sits short of the real one, so keep going until you find the register. Coming down is two to three rappels through the chimney and ramp section, often off fixed slings of unknown age that should be backed up.

sectionBreakdown.note: Same approach as the standard South Peak trip: Saddle Lake Trailhead through old-growth forest and Saddle Lake up to the meadows at Goat Flats. Carry the technical rack and glacier…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Hike in to Goat Flats camp

sectionBreakdown.note: From camp, cross Tin Can Gap and drop roughly 400 ft onto the Queest-Alb Glacier before climbing back up about 1,000 ft to the col between Middle and North Peak. Rope up for sustai…
Break camp at Goat Flats and retrace the trail down through Saddle Lake to the trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: A light rack — slings and a small selection of cams/nuts — is enough for protecting the short 5th-class chimney move; the rest of the route is unroped scrambling.
pro_tips: Carry an ice axe for the upper snow even in summer
The fixed ladders to the lookout are exposed—move carefully
backups.pro_needs: Minimal gear placements needed, concentrated at the one 5th-class chimney move; considerable exposure on this section warrants a rope even though the technical difficulty is modest.
backups.approach: Start at the Tupso Pass trailhead (end of FR 41) on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope (or two ropes if parties want to link stations in fewer pulls). The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
backups.bail: Retreat down the West Couloir/South Face to the glacier is straightforward from most points below the crux chimney; once past the roped 5th-class move, downclimbing or a short rappel off gear may be needed to retreat.

pitch_detail.notes: From Tin Can Gap, drop about 400 ft down steep snow onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Early season it is a plain snow descent. By late summer expect hard, slippery snow or bare ice and a moat where the snow meets the rock, so axe and crampons are needed. Crevasses open by midsummer; rope up when they are snow-covered.

Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft to the col between the Middle and North Peaks. In a high-snow year this goes by a snow tongue and a short couloir of about 40° with moats on both sides. In a low-snow year it becomes loose rock and scree. This climb is the route-finding crux of the day.

Above the col, the climbing is sustained 4th class to a chimney that holds the one real 5th-class move. The rock is loose to fair, so place gear and test holds. Grades given range from Class 4 with a single 5th-class move up to a 40 m lead with harder moves for parties that strayed off the easiest line. An old piton marks one variation.

Above the chimney the ground eases along an exposed, knife-edged crest with big drops east and west. Finish up an easy grassy ramp and over a few blocks to the summit. A short extra low-5th step may be needed depending on the line taken. Rope up for the ridge if the party is unsure: the exposure is serious.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted in late summer (Aug-Sep) once the glacier crossing between Tin Can Gap and the Middle/North col is more consolidated and less crevassed; carry a rope, rack, and glacier gear in addition to standard scrambling kit.

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.notes: Note the access before anything else: the road up to the historic trailhead has a permanent washout, so the day starts with a long bike or walk past the vehicle gate before the trail proper begins. From the trailhead, the trail climbs through forest to the small lake at about two and a half miles — last easy water, and no fires or camping within two hundred feet of it. Continue up into the open meadows of the flats at about four and a half miles, the best camping on the route, then a further couple of miles to the GAP at roughly six miles, where the maintained tread ends and most parties bivy. The gap gives the first real view of the three summits and of the glacier below them.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Crevasses open on the glacier by midsummer and bare ice with a moat appears late in the season; an axe is a year-round item on this peak.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the col
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season, with bare ice by late summer
Loose rock in the chimney and ramp system
No established trail or cairned route above the gap — route-finding is entirely on you
The descent is a committing series of rappels, and some stations are fixed slings of unknown age
Fog on the glacier traverse has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the gap, drop about four hundred feet off-trail down snow and talus onto the glacier, cross it, and CLIMB BACK UP roughly a thousand feet on the far side to the COL BETWEEN THE MIDDLE AND NORTH TOWERS. That col is the base of the climbing, and the thousand-foot re-ascent is the discriminator: this is the only one of the three summits whose route requires you to gain a col before you touch its rock. From the col the line is a RAMP that leads LEFT and then angles RIGHT into a SHALLOW CHIMNEY — the chimney is the check, being the one chimney breaching the block from this col, and it is fourth class with a move or two of low fifth. Above it an exposed fourth-class ridge leads to a grassy ramp and the summit. Negative markers: if you are standing under THREE STACKED WOODEN LADDERS bolted into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the southern end of the ridge, two towers away; if you have climbed a short face straight off the glacier with no col gained, you are on the middle tower's south face.

climbing_route.label: Descent from Tin Can Gap onto the Queest-Alb Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier. Early season this is a straightforward snow descent; by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July). Crevasses open by mid-summer, so rope up as a team when the glacier is snow-covered.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and climb to the Middle-North col
climbing_route.notes: Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak, on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock. This climb is the route-finding crux.

climbing_route.label: Ramp and shallow chimney to the North Peak summit
climbing_route.notes: From the col, follow a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney. Sustained 4th-class with a few low-5th-class exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block. A harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but most parties avoid it for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, rope and harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

gear: Ice axe (recommended into early summer for north-facing snow)
Sturdy boots with good tread for steep heather and slab
Trekking poles for the brushy approach
Map/compass or GPS — travel is cross-country with no maintained trail
Satellite communicator (InReach/Zoleo) given unreliable cell coverage

Steep heather and slab that become slick and hazardous when wet or dewy
Lingering snow and ice on north-facing gullies and slopes into July
