backups.overview: Mutchler Peak (7,150 ft; referenced in some older trip reports as 'Snowqueen') is a remote summit in the Buckindy Group of the Cascade River backcountry, part of the rugged, semi-glaciated ridge system southeast of Marblemount that also includes Snowking Mountain (7,433'), Mount Buckindy (7,320'), Mount Misch (7,435'), Bruseth Mountain (7,220'), and Mount Chaval to the east. There is no maintained trail to Mutchler; it sits in roadless country between the Cascade River and Suiattle River drainages and is almost always climbed cross-country as part of a longer Buckindy Range traverse rather than as a standalone day trip.
backups.beta: Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Parties reach it either by continuing the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past the summit and along the connecting ridge/snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or from the south on the longer Green Mountain–Mount Misch–Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mutchler. Terrain is a mix of steep heather, talus, snow/glacier remnants, and low-class rock; one documented traverse rappelled over a cornice to reach the peak.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, remote approach and the North Cascades' typical afternoon thunderstorm/whiteout risk in summer, set a firm turnaround time to be off exposed ridge and heather terrain by early-to-mid afternoon.
backups.alpine_grade: Mountaineers Scramble S4 / Terrain T5 (rated for the Snowking Mtn NE Shoulder portion that this route climbs first)
backups.rock_grade: 3rd class (one short step, on Kindy Ridge below Snowking's summit)
backups.face: Mutchler Glacier cirque, on Snowking Mountain's southeast ridge
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or reservation. This peak is on Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest land, not in the North Cascades National Park complex.
backups.comms: Deep wilderness terrain far from any road; no reliable cell coverage should be expected in the Kindy Creek/Buckindy interior. Carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: remote terrain with no cell coverage

waypoints.name: FR-1570 Washout Parking (Cascade River crossing)
waypoints.note: Small pullout for 4-5 cars just past a washed-out culvert, 0.4 mi beyond the Cascade River bridge and 1.9 mi off Cascade River Road (FR-15) at mile 14.2 from Marblemount; FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn onto FR-1570, signed for Kindy Ridge and Found Lake, crossing the Cascade River. Park at the washout just past the washed-out culvert — a small pullout with room for four or five cars at about 1,250 ft. FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond this point and the old spur is permanently closed, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek. Cascade River Road access is seasonal and typically gated in winter, and mid-July through September is when the lower slopes are clear enough to be worth the drive.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Roadbed / Way-Trail Start
waypoints.note: The abandoned FR-1570 roadbed (brushy, several windfalls to step over) ends at the edge of an old clearcut where a steep, unmarked way-trail breaks off uphill toward Kindy Ridge.

waypoints.name: Way-Trail Knoll / Kindy Ridge Gain
waypoints.note: The steep boot path tops out on a knoll where the route gains the Kindy Ridge crest; footing is loose and the path is easy to lose in fog or low visibility.

waypoints.name: Kindy Ridge Climbers' Boot Path
waypoints.note: Point on the shared Kindy Ridge climbers' route used by Snowking/Buckindy parties; Mutchler's approach breaks off the ridge here toward Cyclone Lake basin rather than continuing toward Found Peak.

waypoints.name: Cyclone Lake Basin
waypoints.note: Largest and highest of the alpine lakes on Snowking's flanks; established rough campsites on the benches above the lake serve as the usual base camp for Mutchler's summit push, with reliable water from the lake and inlet tarns.

waypoints.name: Heather/Rock Flank Below Summit Block
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed heather-and-rock slope gaining Mutchler's upper flanks — the Class 3 crux referenced in the route grade; can be slick when wet and is the same terrain used on descent.

waypoints.name: Mutchler Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,150 ft; open views west to Snowking Mountain's glaciers and south/east across the Buckindy group peaks (Sonny Boy, Bruseth, Misch, Buckindy).

backups.detailed_rack: No fixed rock rack is documented for this route. The Mountaineers program the Mutchler add-on as a Basic Glacier Climb, so parties carry standard glacier-travel gear (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue hardware, crampons, ice axe) rather than a traditional protection rack.
what_to_bring: extra food/water for a long day
pro_tips: Most parties climb Mutchler as part of a longer Buckindy Range traverse rather than a standalone objective, given the length of the approach
Cyclone Lake (reached via Kindy Ridge) is the standard base camp for Mutchler, Snowking, Buckindy, and Misch — plan a 2-3 day trip rather than a single push

Check current Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF road status before driving; the Cascade River Road washout point near the Kindy Creek/FR 1570 area has persisted for years and can add miles of extra walking or biking
watch_out: Route-finding through the cliff bands below Pt. 5791 is the crux of the standard approach, not the summit scrambling itself
Heather and slab slopes are far more hazardous wet than dry — check weather before committing

backups.pro_needs: Protection needs are glacier-travel oriented (crevasse-rescue kit, and pickets if the Mutchler Glacier crossing warrants them) rather than rock protection; no fixed anchors or bolted protection are documented on the scrambling sections.
backups.best_season: Late July through September, once snow has receded from the approach gullies, cliff bands, and heather slopes. Earlier attempts (June) face lingering snow/ice on north-facing terrain and dangerous, swollen creek crossings on the approach. Because of the long cross-country approach, this is usually planned as a 2-3 day trip combined with neighboring Buckindy Group summits rather than a single-day outing.
backups.approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path about 1.5-1.75 miles, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; total car-to-summit distance is on the order of 12-14 km one way given the ~24.8 km round trip, consistent with reports citing full Snowking/Kindy Ridge trips of 15-17 miles round trip and 6,500-7,100+ ft of cumulative gain. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down Mutchler's heather and blocky rock flanks into the Cyclone Lake basin, then back up and over the Found Peak/Kindy Ridge saddle system to the 4,800 ft saddle and down through the old-growth/windfall section to the firepit and abandoned FR 1570 roadbed, then out to the Cascade River Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — no rappelling is involved on the scramble route or its descent. The main descent hazards are route-finding (the boot path through the meadow/saddle area above Found Peak is easy to lose in both directions and there are cliff bands nearby to avoid), loose rock and heather on the steep upper slopes off Mutchler's summit, and fatigue-driven navigation errors on the long unmaintained stretch back to the road, especially if daylight runs short — at least one trip report specifically mentions avoiding a creek-bed shortcut on the way out after dark in favor of staying on the known road/trail line.
backups.bail: Descend to the approach drainage and follow it back toward the road.

itinerary.cal: Off-trail approach is brushy and best done once most snow has melted off the lower slopes, roughly mid-July through September; the Cascade River Road access is seasonal (typically gated/closed in winter).

days.note: From the Kindy Ridge trailhead at the end of the South Fork Cascade River Road (#1570), follow the blocked/overgrown road then a steep, unmaintained way-trail up Kindy Ridge, staying east of the 5,116' knoll and continuing along Kindy-Found Ridge to a basin camp near Cyclone Pond (~5,450') or the Found Lakes. This is entirely off-trail route-finding through brush and steep timber for the upper portion.

Expect class 2-3 scrambling on the final summit block with route-finding over talus and possible snow patches through early summer; return to the same camp by the same line.

climbing_route.label: Summit block from the basin
climbing_route.notes: From the Kindy Ridge / Cyclone Lake basin, reach Mutchler's summit block by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate class 2-3 scrambling, with some loose rock near the top.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek south fork to the basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the Lake Stuart / Colchuck Lake trail past the fork and leave the maintained tread near the meadow at about 4,500 ft, heading southwest and following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream.

After a couple of miles a steep talus and boulder slope leads into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak. This is the standard camp for the whole north side, and the flat ground itself is the arrival cue.

The glacier has three parts and it is worth knowing them before you set off in the dark: a lower snowfield, the glacier proper, and a steeper couloir in its northwest corner. Parties rope for the short glacier section and take the rope off above it.

This is a compact two-day outing, and it is the line most parties descend after climbing the Ice Cliff Glacier — so if you meet people coming down it at midday they are probably finishing a different climb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul while the glacier still carries continuous snow; it is also the standard early-season DESCENT off the north side, which is when most parties are on it
hazards: Crevasses in the middle section of the glacier and an icefall at its toe
Wet-snow avalanche and rockfall onto the glacier as the day warms
Straying right into the Ice Cliff Glacier's serac fall zone in poor visibility
A steep, unmaintained talus climb into the hanging valley with no trail
Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that move with the snowpack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHERPA IS THE ONE WITH NO ICE ABOVE IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE TEST. Standing in the basin facing the mountain, the three features run in this order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the huge rock rib of the North Ridge.

So the Sherpa is the LEFTMOST — the easternmost — of the two glaciers, and it is the one with nothing hanging over it. The Ice Cliff, immediately to its right, carries an obvious hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. If there is a serac above you, you are one glacier too far right.

TOUCH TEST, and it is the one that works when you cannot see: the ground under the Ice Cliff is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of ice. The Sherpa's toe is ordinary snow over ordinary moraine. Standing on rubble made of ice is direct evidence you have drifted right.

WHERE IT TAKES YOU, as a confirmation rather than a route description: the Sherpa tops out at a notch on Mount Stuart's upper NORTH RIDGE at roughly 7,600 ft, followed by a short scramble. It does not lead to the West Ridge — that is the Stuart Glacier Couloir, on the other side of the rock rib.

And the steep part is in the glacier's NORTHWEST corner, not up its middle. If the steepest ground you can see is straight above the centre of the snowfield, look again at which feature you are under.

climbing_route.label: Lower snowfield and slabs to the glacier toe
climbing_route.notes: From the upper Mountaineer Creek basin, climb the lower snowfield toward the toe of the Sherpa Glacier near 7,600 ft. Once the snow thins, this ground becomes slabs and meltwater streams, and the leftover pocket snowfields above can release rocks onto the slabs, so do not linger below them.

climbing_route.label: Sherpa Glacier
climbing_route.notes: Climb the broad glacier southwest toward the obvious couloir in its northwest corner. The crossing is short and most parties rope up for it. Later in the season, bare ice and rubble piles show through, so weave between them and keep crampons on for the firm morning surface.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund and couloir to the Stuart–Sherpa col
climbing_route.notes: Cross the bergschrund where the glacier narrows. It is filled in early in the season but opens later. Then climb the north-facing couloir up and right to the ridge between Sherpa Balanced Rock and Stuart, near 8,500–8,600 ft. It is high 30s to about 45° and stays shaded, so it can be hard and icy. In lean years it needs front-pointing, and a descent may need rappels.

climbing_route.label: Ridge west to the false and true summits
climbing_route.notes: From the col, follow the ridge west on simple Class 3 blocks. Some ground is taken just on the south side of the crest. The ridge passes above the head of the Cascadian Couloir to the false summit, then continues a short way to the true summit at 9,415 ft. In wind or poor visibility, take careful note of the col so that the glacier descent can be found again.

bivy.notes: The standard base for the north side of Mount Stuart. Leave the Stuart Lake trail before the final switchbacks, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the south fork of Mountaineer Creek to the flat valley below the Sherpa and Stuart glaciers.
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Stuart zone) from May 15 to October 31
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites on flat ground in the basin

backups.name: West Ridge
backups.fa: Lex Maxwell, Fred Llewellyn & John Vertrees, 1935
hazards: Route-finding on a long ridge with several towers and notches
Loose rock in places; exposure on the crest
Long approach and descent make for a big day
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
backups.overview: The easiest technical route up Mount Stuart, a long ridge of mostly 3rd and 4th class with a couple of low-5th steps, first climbed in August 1935 by Lex Maxwell, Fred Llewellyn and John Vertrees. It's a long, athletic day with real routefinding challenges, not a straightforward walk-up.
backups.beta: One of the most popular technical routes on the peak; long and route-finding-intensive, with many opportunities to wander onto harder terrain. Key waypoints: Long John Tower, the West Ridge Notch, then fifth-class rock on the north side to the summit.
backups.turnaround: Turn around by early afternoon; the ridge is exposed and the descent is long and loose.
backups.permit: The Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Creek approach is outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit applies. A free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead box is all that is needed, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Digital Day Pass to park ($5 per day, $30 annually).
backups.descent: Most parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the south side, which offers the shortest and most direct descent to Longs Pass and trailhead. Alternative: downclimb West Ridge (requires caution due to rockfall exposure) or descend Sherpa Glacier to Stuart Lake Trail (early season only).

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737) to its end at the Esmeralda trailhead, about 4,243 ft, and start on the Ingalls Way Trail. Roughly half a mile in, stay right at the Longs Pass junction rather than carrying on toward Ingalls Basin. There is a longer northern approach to this ridge from the Stuart Lake Trailhead over Stuart Pass, but it adds significant mileage and is not the standard line, so Esmeralda is the lot you want.

sectionBreakdown.note: A pre-dawn start over Longs Pass and Stuart Pass reaches the base of the ridge; the ridge itself (5.6) climbs quickly, and the long day is finished off by descending the Cascadian …

backups.detailed_rack: Light alpine rack: a few nuts and small-to-medium cams, alpine draws, a 60 m rope, helmet. Much of the ridge is 3rd/4th class with short 5th-class steps, so a minimal rack suffices for confident parties.

backups.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro for the short 5.4 steps and the False Summit area; mostly a roped scramble for many parties.
backups.best_season: July through September for dry rock; the route is loose but straightforward in summer conditions.
backups.approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.4 mile, stay right/straight at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (5 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing close to 1,000 ft, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. Cross the creek (a straightforward rock-hop or wade in normal summer flow, the last reliable water source before the ridge) and pick up the climber's path heading east/upvalley toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass itself (roughly 6,200–6,400 ft), leave the trail and traverse climber's-left (north) across open talus and heather benches toward the base of the West Ridge — this cross-country traverse is where parties most commonly go astray, since there is no maintained tread and several minor gullies look similar; aim for the obvious deep gully (the middle of three parallel gullies) marked by a large, house-sized boulder at its base. An alternate, longer northern approach via the Stuart Lake Trailhead and Stuart Pass exists but adds significant mileage and is not the standard line. Plan on 3.5–5 hours car-to-base depending on route-finding and snow conditions; some parties camp near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin to break the day up. Hazards: the Longs Pass descent and creek-crossing slopes hold snow into early summer and can be icy at dawn; the final talus traverse to the ridge is loose and exposed to rockfall from parties above; there is no water beyond the Ingalls Creek crossing, so tank up there for the long day ahead. Getting past Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse are the route's main route-finding dilemmas; high on the route, below the summit, a short dihedral with a fixed piton (5.4) or a layback further along the ledge (5.6) leads to easier fifth-class climbing to the top.
backups.descent_text: Descend via the Cascadian Couloir, the standard walk-off for the entire Stuart massif — this is a scramble descent, not a rappel route, under normal (dry to firm-snow) conditions. From the summit, reverse the short 3rd/2nd-class scramble west along the summit ridge to the false summit (~9,200 ft), then drop into the broken rock and scree above the top of the couloir. Stay climber's-right through sparse trees and rock bands near the top to find the true couloir entrance rather than dropping into parallel gullies to the left, which cliff out. From there it's a sustained, direct descent of loose scree/talus (snow early season) losing about 4,000 ft to the floor of the Ingalls Creek valley — many parties glissade or boot-ski the upper snowfield when it's in, which is markedly faster and easier on the knees than the bare-scree version later in summer. Watch for sun cups and inconsistent snow texture on the upper couloir, and expect significant rockfall exposure funneled by the gully, especially with other parties above or below. At the bottom, pick up a climber's path through meadows to the Ingalls Creek Trail near the Longs Pass turnoff, then reverse the approach (back over Longs Pass) to the Esmeralda Trailhead. No rappels are required on this descent in normal conditions; a fixed/natural rock anchor has been reported near the false summit that some parties use to rappel the initial short, steep, icy step off the summit ridge in early-season or verglassed conditions, but this is a discretionary variation, not a standard part of the descent, and the anchor is not maintained or guaranteed. Total summit-to-trailhead time is commonly 3–5 hours for a fit party in good conditions.
backups.bail: Mostly non-committing — you can retreat down the ridge or into the Cascadian at several points. Longs Pass is the exit.

pitch_detail.notes: From the talus shoulder below the ridge, head up the second prominent gully of the parallel set on the south flank rather than the first one encountered. Sandy Class 3 on good granite gives way to steeper scrambling; a short 4th-class chimney exits the top, after which traverse right and slightly down into the next gully, the one beneath Long John Tower. Snow can linger here into midsummer and is often icy early in the day.

Climb to the notch behind Long John Tower. The right side of the face under the tower is the easier way; the alternative is a chimney left of the tower with a chockstone near its start and one strenuous pull. The rock looks steep and loose from below but is solid, sustained Class 4 in reality. Many parties rope up here if the gully holds snow.

The route-finding crux. From the notch, go nearly straight up, then drift right along ledges toward the West Horn rather than following the crest. Pass the Horn on its south side on a broad, very exposed ledge roughly 50 ft below its top; a short belay or handline is common here. Cairns exist on several lines, so follow the terrain rather than the nearest cairn.
pitch_detail.pitch: Long John Tower notch → West Horn

pitch_detail.notes: Keep working right across gullies and ledges to the West Ridge Notch, the second big notch past the Horn, where a small bivy ledge looks straight down onto the Stuart Glacier. Scrambling ends here; most parties rope up for the rest of the climb.

From the notch, climb easy Class 4 a short way, then step left around a blind corner onto the north side of the ridge. Exposure jumps sharply here with the Stuart Glacier far below. Protection is small to medium cams and nuts; a short rope is enough for the whole upper section. Belay where the terrain steepens left of the crest.

Climb steep, blocky low-5th ground just left of the crest to a notch, then cross back to the south side of the ridge. Above, a short low-angle chimney with wide cracks and a brief awkward downclimb lead toward the summit block; several parallel options exist, some harder than the standard line. Keep rope drag down by belaying often.

The technical crux: a short, well-protected pitch up twin finger-to-hand cracks, with a stuck piton at the hardest move. Most parties find it soft for the grade and well protected. Above, easy ground reaches the true summit directly. The descent then heads east along the summit ridge to the false summit to find the Cascadian Couloir.

days.note: A pre-dawn start over Longs Pass and Stuart Pass reaches the base of the ridge; the ridge itself (5.6) climbs quickly, and the long day is finished off by descending the Cascadian Couloir back to the trailhead.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Esmeralda Basin Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737), via the Ingalls Way Trail

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass to upper Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail and, at the junction about half a mile in, stay right for Longs Pass rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin. Switchback up open slopes to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

Descend the steep dusty north side of the pass, losing close to 1,000 ft, and cross Ingalls Creek in the timber below. In normal summer flow this is a rock-hop; it is also the last reliable water before the ridge, so fill up.

Pick up the climbers' path heading east up the valley toward Stuart Pass. You leave it well SHORT of Stuart Pass, in the upper meadows at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft, and traverse climber's-left (north) across talus and heather benches to the foot of the ridge. There is no tread on this traverse and it is the part of the day people get wrong.

Some parties break the approach by camping near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for dry rock; snow lingers on the Longs Pass north side into early summer
hazards: No maintained tread on the talus/heather traverse from the Stuart Pass trail to the ridge — several minor gullies look alike
Steep loose descent off the north side of Longs Pass; icy at dawn in early summer
Loose talus below the ridge with rockfall exposure from parties above
No water past the Ingalls Creek crossing
Descent is the Cascadian Couloir, and 'not staying right' near the top of it is a documented route-finding error
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is identified by counting gullies, not by elevation. Three roughly parallel gullies come down the lower west ridge; the route takes the MIDDLE one, and it is deeper than its neighbours. The confirming feature is at its foot: a single enormous block, described by everyone who has been there as the size of a house, sitting at the base of that gully. If there is no house-sized boulder, you are one gully over.

From the boulder you push up through scrub into the gully and climb up and rightward inside it. The gully ends at a notch — scramble through the notch and Long John Tower is directly in front of you, a distinct pinnacle on the crest. That sighting is the second confirmation that you took the right gully; if you top out of a gully and there is no tower, you are not on the West Ridge.

The climbing past Long John Tower goes up a chimney on the tower's LEFT — about three quarters of a pitch, with a chockstone near the bottom. (An alternative works a short dihedral with a fixed piton, or a layback further along the ledge, before regaining the crest.) Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse beyond it are the two places parties most often stall for route-finding.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers
